doc.title: Ray Bryant interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

chapter: New York working life and business
title: Recording sessions, royalties and record companies
summary: Sessions and pay arrangements, and how record companies cheated musicians of royalties.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: The typical recording session at that time, was it — did they usually give you a couple of days or a couple of sessions in the studio to complete an album?
It was like a three hour session or something. Do you remember how that worked?
Yeah. Maybe three hour sessions and maybe two days. If you needed an extra day you tried to have that set up too.
What was your arrangement with the record label as far as, they pay you for the session and was that the end of it? Did you get money for albums sold?

Well as far as a sideman that was the end of it, yeah. But if you were a leader and it was your recording session then you were supposed to collect royalties, but some of the record companies, you didn’t always collect royalties. You were contracted and you were supposed to collect royalties, but I think most jazz musicians had problems with the recording companies back then. Guys just were not too honest. Hopefully it’s changed a little bit now, but back then, the most you could hope for from, the most you could really rely upon from a recording session was that your record would be out there and get played and you might get some personal engagements from that.
Right. It would be very hard for a musician to keep track of how many records they were selling.
Right. And most guys were not that business-wise to know how to check on it or things like that. Record companies took advantage of it, a definite advantage of it, disgraceful in my estimation.
Was there one record company that had a reputation as being good to work with, honest?

Well I guess your best shot was to try to get with a big company. But no record company was beyond doing certain things. But the best shot would be to get with a big company. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
